title: Vascular dementia
intro: Vascular dementia is a form of dementia caused by reduced blood flow to the brain, often after strokes or damage to small vessels. It affects thinking, planning and mood, and can progress in steps or gradually. Controlling vascular risk factors can slow progress and may prevent it.

sections.heading: Causes
paragraphs: Damage to blood vessels in the brain may be caused by high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, smoking, atrial fibrillation, heart disease and obesity. Large strokes, multiple small strokes or gradual damage to tiny vessels can destroy brain tissue. Vascular dementia can coexist with Alzheimer's disease, as mixed dementia.

sections.heading: Symptoms
paragraphs: Early symptoms often include slowed thinking, difficulty planning and organising, problems with attention and concentration, and changes in mood or personality, with memory affected less early than in Alzheimer's disease. Other signs are walking difficulties, balance problems, urinary urgency and sudden worsening after a stroke. Course varies, with some people stable for periods.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paragraphs: Doctors take a history, examine the person, and use memory and thinking tests. Brain scans with CT or MRI show strokes and vessel damage. Blood tests check for other causes of cognitive decline such as vitamin deficiency or thyroid problems. A specialist may be involved.

sections.heading: Treatment and prevention
paragraphs: There is no cure, and medicines for Alzheimer's disease have limited benefit for vascular dementia unless it is mixed. The most important treatment is controlling risk factors: lowering blood pressure, managing diabetes and cholesterol, treating atrial fibrillation with blood thinners, stopping smoking, regular activity and a healthy diet. Antiplatelet medicines may be given after strokes. Depression and sleep problems should be treated.

sections.heading: Living with vascular dementia
paragraphs: Routine, memory aids, activity, social contact and safe surroundings help. Occupational therapy and rehabilitation maintain independence. Carers need support, information and breaks. Plan early for legal and financial matters, including powers of attorney and care preferences. If a stroke is suspected, call emergency services immediately.

examples.title: Reducing risk
examples.text: Imagine your relative had a small stroke. You could ask the doctor how blood pressure and cholesterol can be controlled and whether blood thinners are needed.

examples.title: Planning ahead
examples.text: Suppose a diagnosis was made recently. You might arrange legal and care planning while the person can still take part in decisions.
